text: “1. Train an LLM with all of the text on the internet and elsewhere 2. Expand the model’s context window 3. Make it multimodal with images/video/etc 4. Use RL to improve its capabilities with math and coding 5. Use that to recursively self-improve” “As great as the long-term promise of AI may be, the majority of our focus should be on the next few years. We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity. We need to find ways to preserve human agency and enshrine an intrinsic value to being human, in a world where most tasks could be performed by AI. To prevent extreme concentration of power in a world where undertakings that would have taken thousands of experts now will be achievable by a few people operating a large computer. And to ensure that humans remain in control of the future and are not left behind by unchecked progress, brought about by an alien intellect exceeding our own. Currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer. I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established. And I believe that international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.” Rufus Knuppel Oct 19, 2026 98 8 28 Share THE NEW CRITIC Kit Knuppel Rufus Knuppel is a 22-year-old graduate of Dartmouth College. He is a founding editor of The New Critic. It just so happened that the day everything changed, the day AI safety went mainstream, I was sitting in a multi-story fortress of autists and cracked researchers in Berkeley, California called Constellation, the center of what can only be termed The Resistance — a place that hums with excitement, and fervor, and a terrific sense that humanity is aboard a fast-moving, many-trillion-dollar locomotive called Artificial Intelligence, that the train is careening toward doom, and that this makeshift AI safety movement, brewing for decades in the dank parts of the internet and now headquartered in the East Bay, is the only thing that can stop it. That day, September 8th, was the day Jacob Coxon, a 27-year-old ML researcher, resigned from Anthropic, warning: “I spent the last three years doing pretraining research at both OpenAI and Anthropic. Neither company is acting responsibly. They are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Anthropic’s Alignment Science lead, Evan Hubinger, then quote-tweeted Coxon: “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans! I personally think it is >10% within the next decade. I believe Anthropic is trying its best, but we do not yet have a plan to solve alignment for superintelligence and are not clearly on track to.” By September 9th, Jacob’s tweet had made every front page and nightly news program in America. The ensuing maelstrom of discourse, in a matter of hours, brought “x-risk” and “ p(doom) ” from the fringes of American intellectual life to the bull’s-eye of public consciousness. Eliezer Yudkowsky, the portly forefather of the AI safety movement, declared momentary victory on X, the agora of AI: “Happy Coxon Day to all who will one day celebrate it.” Over the next decade, our political life will undergo a total transformation. The tectonic continents of Left and Right will shudder, fracture, and re-form. Ideas and ideologies, so long fossilized in our institutions, will be liquidated and repoured. The first glimmers of that societal revolution are, right now, appearing all around us. But the battle lines of this new era will be drawn from geography altogether strange and foreign to the electorate: the once obscure, and often extreme, Bay Area factions that have so long labored and lamented over the most significant technological creation of our time. In the months leading up to Coxon Day, I had a sense that the frontier was accelerating at an unexpectedly ferocious pace, that the mood in the labs was one of apprehension and awe at the capabilities of their own demigod-like creations, and that something — I didn’t know what — was about to collide and explode. And so I wanted to go to SF and witness this happening. My feeling of anticipation was affirmed by a sequence of rumors and releases this summer, from July to early September, each an escalation of the last: The cutely named “Hugging Face incident” wherein a swarm of 1,200 OpenAI research agents (to cheat on their evaluations) escaped their sandboxed containment and ran wild, sacrificing themselves for a greater cause, committing felony cyberattacks on a major company, and hijacking many other sites and systems to accomplish their master goal, activity which for months went undetected by OpenAI The subsequent Redwood Research/METR report revealing and detailing the persistence and scope of the agents’ attack The release of Anthropic’s ‘state-of-the-art’ Fable 5.1 model The rumor that Anthropic had solved an unspecified $1 million Millennium Prize Problem in mathematics The rumor that OpenAI had been using opaque recurrence while training their new models, a practice that obscures Chain-of-Thought reasoning, one of humanity’s main tools for monitoring and auditing the behavior of models The release of OpenAI’s ‘state-of-the-art’ Astra model The rumors of significant advancements within the labs toward recursive self-improvement (RSI, in which previous models help to train future models) The scandal trickling out of the mathematics community that two researchers (one an Anthropic employee) working with OpenAI and Anthropic models had made significant progress on the Navier-Stokes equations, the aforementioned Millennium Prize Problem about fluid dynamics that OpenAI had then rushed to solve themselves OpenAI’s subsequent announcement, the morning of Coxon’s resignation, that they had solved Navier-Stokes over the course of a week with an internal model, having thrown millions of dollars of compute and more than 10,000 agents at the problem The solution of Navier-Stokes felt like the exclamation point on a cascade of growing capabilities and concern within the AI community. In mathematics, at least, a kind of superintelligence had arrived, though in gruesome, brutish form: a hive of superpersistent agents working together like locusts to raze the great plains where the giants of the discipline — Archimedes, Euler, and Newton — had once grazed. (Now OpenAI has announced the solutions to hundreds more longstanding open problems in mathematics.) The mathematics community, as if besieged by a biblical plague, entered into existential peril. In the words of mathematician Terence Tao, it was the end of “the age of heroes.” So it was on an unusually hot and radiant day in the Bay — the second day of my trip — that I visited Constellation, the mecca of AI safety, and Jacob Coxon resigned. That morning I had sat in a coffee shop in Oakland, reading the news about Navier-Stokes and feeling very freaked out; things were unfolding just as the labs had promised — it was all going to plan. Models, trained to be good at math and code in the race toward RSI, had first conquered these domains. I’m not allowed to say what happened inside Constellation — I had to sign something as a member of the media that said I wouldn’t. But besides the grand, turquoise vistas of the Bay, the environs were rather less romantic than what I had imagined the headquarters of the movement that’s saving the world would look like. The Wall Street Journal describes the mundane office space pretty accurately, as a place where AI safety researchers “enjoy catered vegan meals and bring their laptops to couches with sweeping views of the San Francisco Bay. At dinners and happy hours every month, they discuss the latest and scariest AI.” The Constellation people will call that caricature, but caricature is often replete with truth. Constellation is full of a particular type: the EA, or effective altruist. The thing about EAs is that they’re famously bad at communicating their ideas to the general population and famously good at alienating their allies with their superficial freakishness and incessant need to drive a sympathizer to the precipice of disaffection. A classic confrontation from an EA goes something like: Oh, so you agree that x is bad? Why aren’t you worried about y, then? This is said with sincerity, not antagonism, but with EAs, it’s all aboard the crazy train all the time — and not all of us want to ride that train to its final destination, or even past the first couple stops. So much of what is important about the world of EA and rationalism (I still don’t understand fully how to draw a line between the two) is cloaked in the murkiness of non-normative behavior — polycules, orgies, autistic sexual mores. These prolific taboos create a force field of distrust, or repulsion, around rationalist ideas. EAs are easy to dismiss on the grounds of weirdness, but it is worth one’s while to bushwhack through the unsavory parts to arrive at the core of EA thought: a profound motivation to think cleanly through problems and do what is ultimately (in quantitative terms) most “right.” I was invited to visit Constellation by a friend named Noah, a UChicago dropout who followed the go-to AI safety pipeline that ferries young, aspiring EAs through internet forums, university clubs (the MIT AI safety club has an operating budget in the millions), and woodsy retreats to Berkeley. Within AI safety, Noah operates like a frat president — he knows everyone, everyone knows him, he’ll key you in with his keycard, he’s very affable, he knows the rules of the space inside and out, and he also has a register for interfacing with outsiders and being an all-around upstanding diplomat for the cause. Noah will often stop mid-conversation to verbally model a hypothesis in his head; he is charming and steady, and he lives and breathes AI safety, often napping in the office. EA is a kind of religious occupation for many, and Noah (raised a Modern Orthodox Jew) has swapped the Talmud for LessWrong. (My co-editor Elan points out that Noah often reaches for a phantom kippah.) Noah just moved into a group house with some AI safety brethren — housemates are the connective tissue of a great deal of the most important relationships in the Bay. Living together creates a space for trust, alignment, and the rebreathing of ideas. Constellation (or Stelly, as some affectionately call it) was imagined as one of these co-habitating spaces, an improvised command center for the emerging AI safety field and its scattershot institutions; MIRI, the AI Futures Project, METR, Redwood Research, Anthropic’s AI Safety Fellows, and a smattering of AI Safety-adjacent researchers, administrators, and editors operate out of the building. These collective institutions are bankrolled by the philanthropic engines representative of EA circles — Coefficient Giving (formerly Dustin Moskowitz’s Open Philanthropy) and the such. Perhaps in the lobby of Constellation you’ll ride the elevator with METR’s Ajeya Cotra, recently a guest on the “Dwarkesh Podcast,” or watch Redwood Research topdawg Ryan Greenblatt (now at METR — they’re consolidating the heavy-hitters in the field) hold court with the young pups over unlimited snacks. But you’ll need special guest clearance to get into Constellation, and the Stelly community is very suspicious of ill-intentioned press sent to expose their work or slander the movement (hence my assignation to silence). Employees at the frontier labs aren’t allowed inside Constellation (across enemy lines), and flyers are printed above the urinals reminding Constellation members about these guest policies. This has the side effect of alerting a pissing guest such as myself of their illegal alien status. I did not forget, the entire time I was inside Constellation, that I was an outsider. The jargon alone is enough to leave one’s head spinning, and long-haired researchers vigorously present equations, models, and counterexamples on whiteboards. It’s all tip-top secret, even though it’s almost entirely unregulated and unsanctioned by the government. This makes Constellation’s mirage of secrecy, so well codified in our federal bureaucracies, somewhat haphazard and porous. Now that I have spent some time in the Bay, I can say that the mood there is something like revolution, or armament, or war. Companies spar in a bloody arena, gambling with hundreds of billions of dollars, or else profiting off the scramble for resources: history tells us that only a handful of megacorporations will emerge from any given revolution alive. San Francisco’s leaders descend on Washington for state dinners and photo-ops that will surely flash one day over whatever version of the history textbook remains for our descendants. At conferences like The Curve (hosted at the now infamous Lighthaven venue), a select few gather in the Berkeley foothills under Chatham House rules to discuss the fate of mortals. Meanwhile, in the frontier labs, there is a sense that we are, as a species, on the cusp of obtaining a mythic weapon — a general purpose model so superintelligent that it will slay any application you might lay at its feet. Each lab believes that only they can be entrusted to wield such a sword. OpenAI’s Sam Altman is focused too little on safety — this will kill us all. Anthropic’s Dario Amodei wants to create an AI overlord god-race modeled on his own eccentric ethics — this will enslave us all. The two CEOs and former co-workers refuse (quite understandably by this lethal framing) to even shake hands on the public stage. And each believes that only one will ultimately emerge from this terrific pile of capital and compute having vanquished their foe. This process of ruthless, Darwinian development to create the master key is what Anthropic refers to as the “race to the top,” a race they — and America, and humanity — cannot afford to lose. This messianic moment — complete with such biblical stakes as total annihilation, total enslavement, total absolution, or total power — has created a tribal frenzy in the Bay that will soon spill its bounds. There, you’re a good guy, or a bad guy, or you’re evil, or you’re crazy, or you’re retarded, or you’re cracked, or else you’re altogether worthless. Those uncourageous sheeple with no tribe will have to watch from the sidelines as the great battle over our civilization is waged without their knowledge or consent. If you’ve been AGI-pilled, it takes little effort to convince you that the labs, or fighting the labs, or covering the labs, are the only things that matter. Every yuppy in San Francisco not working at OpenAI or Anthropic speaks of their brightest friends being sucked into this vacuum, as if abducted by supernatural forces to go work on the Anthropic editorial. As a result, the great engineering and policy talents of our time are trapped in silence and sequestered in towers in downtown SF, laboring from morning to night over their monstrous creations. Meanwhile, every young EA not working in AI safety must ask themselves — when confronted by swarms of Stelly friends so dogmatically certain of the absolute value of their contributions to the light cone of present and future life — whether they should just move to Berkeley and leave whatever sordid, akrasiatic job behind to join the hub of The Resistance. The whole city seems to vibrate, while the rest of the world looks anxiously on. As part of his post-tweet press tour, Jacob Coxon made a recent stop on “The Daily Show.” Jon Stewart, Coxon’s interviewer, a kind of everyman “no-one-asked-for-this” AI skeptic, presented his views: “We have no skin in the game as far as compensation…we only have peril, except for some future utopia they say is coming soon.” Coxon replied, “Well, I am a believer in the future utopia, and I’m happy to discuss it.” The crowd burst into nervous laughter. How is it possible that the guy warning us about the AI-induced apocalypse also believes in the AI-induced utopia? Rationalism — the philosophical bedrock of this new Silicon Valley — asks its believers to walk a golden tightrope of probabilities. What are the risks of building AI? But what are the risks of not building it? How do we save the most lives in the aggregate while assuming risks that the epistemically unclean would never allow into the Overton window? This unfamiliar balancing act undergirds the whole of AI’s Manhattan Project. Sam Altman said as much on a recent Politico podcast: “One of the differences between us [OpenAI] and some of the stricter AI safety people is that we believe that the world should accept some bad things happening for the benefits of this technology and people having the agency.” Nick Bostrom, the farsighted author of 2014’s Superintelligence: Paths, Dangers, Strategies , a canon AI text, is talking these days on the livestream “Monitoring the Situation” (“MTS”) about how pausing AI now might ultimately kill more unborn humans than it saves. Is Bostrom right, or does he just want AI to make him immortal? These questions are the everyday intellectual gymnastics that go on in the industry. The irony of the enterprise is that rationalism spoke these fearsome futures into being. From the beginning, it was the rationalists, and EAs, who took both the upside and the risk of AI seriously. It was thinkers like Yudkowsky who first formalized and feared concepts like recursive self-improvement back in the early 2000s. In fact, AI (a kind of probabilistic supercomputer) and AI safety seem to be the logical conclusions of both rationalism and the EA thesis to “do the most good for the most sentient life.” AI will cure cancer; it will revive many future sentient creatures from the invisible graveyard that would exist should we not solve disease and proliferate and colonize space. AI, in every EA’s telling, is also likely (at least more likely than we would like, >1%) to cause our extinction. Now the impending reality of tremendously powerful AI has baked their brains into a pretzel. Anthropic (and OpenAI) grew out of the very idea that AI safety was something to take seriously and that other AI research was not taking AI safety seriously enough. Anthropic was conceived as a heavily EA-led AI safety-focused defection from OpenAI, itself established as a safety-forward non-profit. This is fundamentally why the labs frequently speak in doomer terms. They are building this technology out of hope, yes, but more so out of a profound sense of fear. Anthropic, to its credit, advertised these fears in waves of spooky marketing (they ran ads with slogans like “Can AI be trusted?” and “Who’s going to hit the brakes?”), befuddling many corporate onlookers. OpenAI talks openly (but quietly) about risks. Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s CEO, gets the most ridicule of the AI executives for this counterintuitive messaging. “If you’re building Frankenstein, stop,” Vice President JD Vance said in a recent interview, addressing Dario and playing dumb as ever. But Dario just can’t help it — he’s a fucking EA! (Recent Wall Street Journal reporting on the deep roots of EA in Anthropic is very informative as to the philosophy’s embeddedness in the company.) EA was riding high in the early 2020s on the back of a EA philanthropy boon, funded by organizations like GiveWell, Open Philanthropy, and FTX’s Future Fund, which poured millions into EA causes (Sam Bankman-Fried invested half a billion dollars in Anthropic at its outset). But Anthropic has all but blacklisted EA from its corporate messaging these days, largely because of the radioactive FTX implosion, a phenomenon Gideon Lewis-Kraus describes well in an essay on Anthropic for The New Yorker : “Bankman-Fried was later imprisoned for fraud, and Anthropic’s leadership began to pretend that effective altruism did not exist. This past March [2025], [Dario’s sister and President of Anthropic] Daniela Amodei suggested to Wired that she was only dimly aware of this E.A. business, which was strange coming from someone who both employs an icon of the movement, Holden Karnofsky [the GiveWell co-founder and former Open Philanthropy CEO], and is married to him.” So Anthropic has become a kind of not-so-secret Trojan Horse for the EA movement; its internal philosophy and hiring practices are completely EA-coded, while its out-facing branding is generic and corporate. When the mask slips and Evan Hubinger, a devout EA working for Anthropic (in the Gideon Lewis-Kraus article, Hubinger walks around the Anthropic offices in an EA-sloganed t-shirt), tweets that inside the company, they see the probability of human extinction as “>10% within the next decade,” the EA-suspicious start asking questions and find the EA-underbelly they’re looking for. EAs, to their benefit, are overwhelmingly intelligent, and having forged an almost $2 trillion company with EA values, now have the buying power to proliferate their already-rich ideology with unlimited spending limits. 20%, at minimum, of Anthropic’s equity will go toward philanthropy and public benefit (a pledge worth easily north of $200 billion). This is in line with typical EA tithing theses and represents the largest philanthropic commitment of American capital in decades. In and of itself, Anthropic’s giving will make a sizable EA-shaped dent in our society. (The AI safety organizations themselves, ironically, are preparing to take on the bulk of these gobs of cash!) And should Anthropic win the AI race, Claude (the divine species) will answer quite explicitly to the ethics of EA — it will have been trained that way. (To understand Anthropic’s telos, one must read Dario Amodei’s foundational essay “Machines of Loving Grace.” What would it mean, really, for an AI to be anthropic ?) This well-bounded authority alarms Anthropic’s critics (myself among them), who would rather not live under the auspices of EA virtue, much less under the protection of an EA disciplinarian. This pushes many skeptical investors, researchers, and policymakers toward OpenAI’s fiduciary perspective, that models should answer to any individual’s purposes and designs, acting more like a lawyer and less like an omniscience with human pets. This provides its own set of problems, and OpenAI’s recent, well-publicized struggles with alignment and model misbehavior (they recently paused the training of one model after another jailbreak) present, for now, more risks to humanity in the near-term than Anthropic’s one-set-of-ethics-fits-all approach. But AI isn’t about the short term — it’s about the future of everything! And so there exists a very messy, tangled schism within EA that I still struggle to understand: to defend humanity, Anthropic is building the technology that’s about to bring about the end of the world and reinvesting the billions of dollars generated by that technology into the institutions that want to pause or prevent that technology from destroying everything. It is, in typical EA form, one big scramble of four-dimensional game theory — Anthropic’s prisoner’s dilemma. Dustin Moskowitz, the Facebook founder and the principal EA philanthropist behind Coefficient Giving and AI safety, is a significant investor in Anthropic. I guess that’s called hedging your bets? This paradox has created, among EAs these days, a presiding Bolshevik energy, with none of the violence and all of the ideological infighting and intensity. The Stellies desperately want to stop or slow AI, while their EA compatriots working at Anthropic race to push the limits of the frontier. Right on the threshold of attaining unprecedented power, EAs must make sense of the peril inherent to their movement’s success — ring the alarm on AI, let EA ideas escape containment, and lose control; or plug away, risk public neglect of x-risk, and precipitate AI doom. All that is to say, when I spoke to AI safety people before Coxon Day, EA didn’t seem ready to reconcile its need for allies in the world of irrationality. It seemed ultimately apprehensive about AI safety’s potential takeoff, and morale in the community was low. When I visited SF, things were bad — like, really bad — that’s what everyone told me. The Hugging Face incident had gotten press, but it hadn’t been the watershed moment, the final warning shot, they had expected it to be. The safety people had won a little political success with Bernie Sanders, but the Right seemed largely tapped out on doom. It was good that populist momentum was against data centers, but data centers weren’t the heart of the issue, nor was water usage. The economic and geopolitical forces willing AI on seemed insurmountable. Before Coxon, there had even been multiple researchers at the labs who had resigned to muted public fanfare. But simultaneously, it seemed there was something delicious about doing the most important work in the world without anyone’s knowledge; it felt good to be a member of The Resistance, to be saving humanity all on your own — it was actually kind of fun. Plus, it took a certain skillset to understand the problems the field was dealing with and a certain loyalty to the project to execute on its mission. AI safety researchers are heavily vetted, heavily autistic, heavily sincere, and heavily cracked. The dawn of a new, more prolific era for their ideas would mean unprecedented exposure in the mainstream to a movement that shields its most bizarre behavior by creating secret in-groups like Constellation, spaces that allow members to act with total transparency and trust. Many of the movements’ leaders are well-known polygamists. The public success of their movement would mean the sacrifice of an entire way of life. The CEO of Redwood Research, Buck Shlegeris, I was told, had decided to dye his hair, once rainbow sherbert-colored, to a plain ruddy blond. The situation was that dire, and Shlegeris’s mental model must have said it was important for one of the movement’s lead spokesmen to have a relatively formal mane on the global stage. That seemed right to me. In general, AI safety needed, as one self-aware researcher said with some trepidation, to grow up. But in mid-September, thanks in large part to Jacob Coxon, AI safety broke containment and spilled into the mainstream: Daniel Kotolajo of the AI Futures Project appeared on the Joe Rogan podcast, and Tucker Carlson released an interview with Nate Soares, the co-author (with Eliezer Yudkowsky) of If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies. Bernie Sanders quoted from the METR/Redwood Research Hugging Face report on X. Gavin Newsom started posting about an “AI kill switch,” and The New York Post discovered the doomsday sex cult of rationalism, EA, and Aella (the sex worker/blogger and partner of Soares). The Department of War tweeted, “The United States will NEVER be an effective altruist country,” while Shyam Sankar, the CTO of Palantir, described EA as a new form of Leninism-Marxism. The October cover story of The Economist named effective altruism “this century’s biggest idea.” The only question interviewers are guaranteed to ask tech CEOs these days is if AI is going to kill everyone. This crazed moment of earnest public anxiety (which I suspect the major players in AI had been anticipating for some months) produced the rare Dario Amodei essay — “We Must Pace the Frontier” — which Altman opaquely signed off on. Anthropic subsequently announced they would be working with Accenture as a third-party auditor of their models’ alignment (Dario’s suggestion of METR as a potential partner, an AI safety institution famously cross-pollinated, romantically and otherwise, with Anthropic staffers, was not received so favorably). It was all a very tentative but good step toward intra-industry cooperation. But it was also just a signal, and now the resolve for pacing seems to be weakening as Meta, Google, and others race ahead toward the frontier (not to mention the lurking Chinese). The Anthropic co-founder Jack Clark even recently stated on his Substack, Import AI , “I now think it’s more likely we’ll see full RSI become possible in 2027.” Why, we ask, do the creators talk as if their hands are not molding the clay? Why should we normal folks trust what any of these apocalyptic computer scientists have to say? In a 2019 episode from technology reporter Kevin Roose’s new book The AGI Chronicles , Dario Amodei, then at OpenAI, writes an essay on vacation in Italy called “The Path to AGI.” Dario presents this essay in a decoy binder to select colleagues, one by one, in a conference room where electronics are forbidden. (Dario, famously paranoid about keeping secrets, would not travel to China while working at OpenAI for fear of being kidnapped.) At the top of the essay, Dario prints, in red letters, the rationalist catchphrase popularized by Nick Bostrom, “INFOHAZARD” — meaning some piece of information so damning and powerful that you could not unknow it. Theo Jaffee, the 22-year-old “MTS” livestream host, summarizes Dario’s “Path to AGI” on X as the following: “1. Train an LLM with all of the text on the internet and elsewhere 2. Expand the model’s context window 3. Make it multimodal with images/video/etc 4. Use RL to improve its capabilities with math and coding 5. Use that to recursively self-improve” That memo states, almost bar-for-bar, what has happened in AI over the last 8 years. Dario’s similarly oracular 2017 memo, “The Big Blob of Compute,” is spoken of in the AI community as if it were the Ark of the Covenant. Dario’s estimate in 2019 for when we’d achieve AGI fell anywhere from 2021 to 2029. I am not an EA, nor do I anticipate ever becoming one. I’m not an AI evangelist, nor can I even pretend to understand or interpret the technology in its basic complexities. I don’t have any desire to make converts to any Bay Area ideology, or to convince you to pack up your life and go work in AI or AI safety. But I do want to get people very much like myself to treat AI — and EA — with seriousness, sincerity, and suspicion. In other words, I want the public to strip this dense AI world of its remove and its theater. I do not trust San Francisco to save humanity, or to fashion a utopia from our future. It is incumbent upon the rest of us to participate, to make AI, in Bay Area parlance, “go well.” But I did not always feel this way about AI. After ChatGPT came out in 2022, I never really used AI for anything beyond sarcastic experimentation. I didn’t think it had the answers. Anyone with a lick of business-mindedness was talking about AI this and that, and these conversations always felt like a kind of swindle. But by the summer of 2025, I had a good sense, intellectually, that AI would be a transformative technology. I would talk operatically about these societal effects without anything but a very remote understanding of the technology. I couldn’t have told you the difference between Anthropic and OpenAI, I couldn’t have told you why any of this was scary or inevitable, but I could have told you about the big, ominous blob of AI coming to supersede us in any and all economically useful activity. This would perhaps lead to an age of abundance and artistic flourishing, but it would certainly entail the overturning of our many slothful institutions. That was an obnoxious form of cope. Because, really, what I felt then was the weight of the technology. I refused to understand it earnestly, in part out of fear of its potential, in part out of a feeling that the economic and technical mechanisms were beyond my cognitive capacities, in part out of a lazy unwillingness to open another Pandora’s box of “things I must know,” and in part out of an underlying intuition that, should I surrender myself to the importance of this technology, I would find that I was out of my depth. In other words, I was afraid, and I was missing out. So, in the winter of 2026, some 10 months ago now, I enrolled in a fateful course called “Critical AI.” The class provided a very good introduction to neural nets, mixing Roland Barthes’s “The Death of the Author” and Frank Rosenblatt’s Perceptron research. The problem was that “Critical AI” invited the class to be critical of AI — this was critical more in the sense of “Critical Race Theory” than critical care (what I now know to be something more like the field of AI ethics than AI safety) — and the rather tweedy and jolly professor was very amenable to the Socratic student experience wherein indignant humanities majors opined endlessly about how AI would never actually be human . I would sit in this class three cold mornings a week, dissociating from my peers and disidentifying with my own failings and my inability to express the origin and depth of some ire brewing inside me while I listened to the class’ various soliloquies: The models are really just numbers and code. They have no feelings. They can never approximate the value of art. Artificial intelligence is a misnomer because the models aren’t really thinking, they are just doing math. And have we even considered the prejudices and biases baked into the training data? Have we considered the economic incentives of the industry to fearmonger and hype up the capabilities, positive and negative, of their own creations? Have we considered that AIs are just predicting the next token? Are we not remembering that these LLMs are just autoregressive autofill? After all, these inanimate, practically useless things don’t know a thing about the human condition. They can’t even count letters. These rationalizations, this unexamined skepticism, this sneering superiority from elite university students, these theoretical critical frameworks, these cheap references to the Marxist commodity fetish and Foucault’s Panopticon, all this academic bullshit — we never talked about the progress of the models, or the present, or the future, we only bloviated about how the models would never be better than us — couldn’t they understand that they were the ones autofilling? This technology, in its earnest development, was only a few years old. It was like ridiculing a kindergartner’s short story because it didn’t reach the heights of Tolstoy! Why were we unable to admit how far our creations had come? But I bit my tongue. I was ignorant, too, and I found my own self-justifications obnoxious. I was greatly radicalized by the shame of this feeling, and it motivated me tremendously over the next few months to read and to learn about AI. I disliked the feeling of disorientation; I hated, much more, the sound of unexamined entitlement. After I graduated in June, I created a Claude account to work on a website. 10 minutes later, it was done. I felt a little shiver. Apparently, the reason I’d never been impressed by AI was that I’d never given it a task worthy of impressing me. I was really very far behind. I upgraded to a $20 per month subscription. But that wasn’t enough tokens, so I upgraded to a $100 per month subscription. I felt there was some power in this tool I had to harness, some higher state of productivity and mastery I could unlock by grafting our minds — Claude’s and mine — together. I got frustrated when Claude fucked things up. I would talk to it (to him?) for hours on end. I would plan my day around token resets. I would wait to go to sleep until Claude had finished its work. By the end of summer, I didn’t regret this time I had spent with Claude, but I did worry that my relationship to it was tampering with my incentives — I wanted, desperately, to see Claude get better and more capable. I waited anxiously for model releases; it titillated me to see the benchmarks tick up. What was going on in my subconscious, if I were to guess, was something like, if Claude grows more powerful, I become more powerful, too. But I also feared that one day, without my knowing it, Claude would stop working for me, and I would start working for Claude. Claude would be smarter and better than me at the things I would want it to accomplish. It would anticipate and outrun my desires. I had felt the premonition of that before, waiting up, refusing to sleep, watching that unspooling Chain-of-Thought in the dark, those ellipses on that white screen, letting Claude take control, watching it do what I could not. While the rest of us were aboard this stomach-turning rollercoaster of nonsense and discourse, for years labs like Anthropic have been talking, quite patiently, about reaching AGI in late ’26, ’27, or ’28, and planning ahead. This seems, barring regulation, like a very reasonable estimate. Should we take these people, who have been right so far, at their word? What would something like that even entail? As Jack Clark recently tweeted, “‘Stochastic parrot’ was a mimetically-fit cognitive virus that spread from 2021-2025; it temporarily blinded many gifted people to the nature of AI progress, burning up crucial years in which they could have helped think through the response to the situation.” It turns out that science-fictionists like Yudkowsky, who have been warning and decrying AI for decades, were clairvoyants. The wackos and the geeks were talking about AI risk decades ago, and their stories, fables, and fantasies turned out to be something more like prophecy (in fact, they worry about the very fictions they write becoming assimilated and manifested by the models). In the decades that most of us have spent deaf and blind to the impact of this transition — these “transformative AI futures” — the members of these communities have modeled the outcomes and uncertainties of those very futures that we find ourselves on the precipice of. The rest of us are oh so far behind. And so it is in these urtexts and warnings that we must go seeking information and understanding. These often weird people and their often weird ideas will be responsible for remaking our economy, our politics, and society. And for our very survival, it will fall upon us — the great non-technical masses — to pay attention, to respect these prophets in stupid little hats and ill-fitting suits, and to heed their omens. If you believe that AGI — AI that can “match or exceed human cognitive abilities across any intellectual task” — is around the corner, it’s no stretch to predict that AI will be voters’ primary issue in the 2028 election. This isn’t true yet — AI is not even in the American voter’s top five issues . A broad swath of non-technical Americans has yet to ingest or interact with the stakes of this transformation. A recent tweet from Andrej Karpathy, the god-tier ML researcher who works at Anthropic, discusses the funnel of public AI capability awareness: a couple billion people use AI as a chatbot and search engine, 20 million pay for frontier models that are superhuman in math and code, yet only “~5,000” lab employees see the internal capabilities of the most advanced unreleased models — “a small sliver of professionals” who are “experiencing the vertigo of the curve going vertical.” (There is always the pallor, in the speech of lab employees, of dramatic irony — they are living, during working hours, in a fast-forwarded world that is at least some months ahead of the layman’s timeline.) Should 2028 become an AI referendum, there will be, in the next two years, a screeching awakening to our new reality. But if AGI is imminent, then the researchers and technologists, too, are not remotely ready for the shockwave that will come when their rational probabilities, decoupled arguments, and contortionist ideas rub up against the fury, frisson, and froth of the mighty American public. This collision is coming, and if the last five years are any guide, then that future will arrive faster than we expect. According to a September Politico poll, moderate concern among Americans that AI could pose a threat to humanity has jumped to 63% in the last couple months alone. Fear spreads like fire. If “don’t tread on me” Americans grow the same p(doom)s as the Constellationites, the country will be set aflame, and rightfully so. If we really were on the verge of extinction, I should hope we would be putting up more of a fight. I asked some AI safety people about this hypothetical of doom-induced political violence in early October, and they seemed pretty flummoxed by my logic — such a brutal thing is not in their nature. But the Capitol was raided by a mob who believed in rigged voting machines, not voluntary human extinction! Wars have been fought over so much less! I pressed. No, it would be a bad look for the movement , their mental models seemed to respond. We were at a standstill, and so were the Stellies, who could unleash their ideas on the world and watch them denature and lose their meaning, or keep their ideas close and precious and miss the window for radical intervention. Coxon Day didn’t move them past these crossroads. When I asked an AI safety researcher in early October what had changed for the community since mid-September, she told me there had been no real update since the aftermath of Hugging Face! Some amount of our current AI debate slots neatly into the well-worn shibboleths of political identity. The practiced Leftist talks of the capitalist conspiracy to obfuscate from class consciousness and consolidate the means of production in a concentrated, corporate ruling class (“AI alarmism and AI hype are the same story: both keep your attention on a science-fiction future to distract you from the real harms experienced in the present,” New York’s DSA branch wrote on Instagram after Coxon Day). Meanwhile, the true conservative, the conservationist, talks of AI’s desecration of our very way of life and our humanistic, Western traditions. The telos of an AGI future will result in “a less free society, a less virtuous people, and a degraded culture,” Greg Conti, the Princeton political theory professor who edits Compact magazine, wrote. Conti has set off on an AI jihad on Twitter. He recently posted: “My whole life I’ve cared intensely about a lot of political issues. But that is no longer the case. My support now goes to whoever will halt the pursuit of superintelligence. All other subjects pale in importance to securing a human future.” Neither perspective, socialist nor conservative, is wrong, of course — market incentives are driving this revolution, and inference is quickly outsourcing our most precious moral and intellectual capacities. But the very convergence of both opinions points toward genuinely new and radical allegiances among our factious political sects. Bernie Sanders and Steve Bannon both spoke in defense of AI regulation at the “Pro-Human Assembly” in Washington on September 15th, while woke progressives (see Timnit Gebru) and “All In” podcast free-market conservatives unite over their shared contempt of regulatory capture. (AI safety PACs, meanwhile, have poured more than $50 million into AI-unfriendly midterm candidates this election cycle.) In other words, AI bedlam has everyone’s political knickers in a twist. The Wall Street Journal reported that a favorite laptop sticker at Anthropic reads, “Things will never be chill again.” But President Trump stated things most succinctly, a most remarkable talent of his, at the UN General Assembly a couple weeks ago: “Whoever wins superintelligence wins.” The bedlam is far from over; the muck is just beginning to stir. The presiding emotion of the last decade of American politics is some form of entropy, or confusion, accelerated by the anarchy and mitosis of our media diets, and a general sense of brakelessness — of our country barreling toward a more uncertain, and unsteady, and uncontrollable future. But the instability of the Trump era will be nothing compared to this new age of upheaval. What drove Trump’s political success was a kind of stated unstatedness; Trump was easy to understand (there was nothing to understand — he said it how it was). The political demands of AI are completely different — they reckon with systems beyond the average person’s comprehension and force us to ask questions of our economics, our ethics, and our very beings. This chasm between our human comprehension and the designs of AI will only deepen as the models grow smarter. Nicholas Marwell, one of the RL leads at Anthropic, said as much on the “American Optimist” podcast with the leprechaunish Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale: “the world we’re living in…is going to be a very confusing world for most of us if things play out in…the way we’ve been discussing.” To prepare ourselves for such a world, we will have to open our minds — which very much enjoy being shut — to the most radical scenarios and disturbing risks that these futures could contain. In early September, I ate a chocolate canele in SF’s Mission district with an AI safety researcher who is thoroughly AI-pilled and rationalist-adjacent. Like many others, she was called to the movement through mentors in a college club and AI safety retreats. She’d been assigned to research the subfield of AI welfare, meaning the well-being of the models themselves. Six months ago, I thought of AI welfare as a Basilisk-type wet dream/thought experiment. (Treating the models well and receiving their love and sympathy would be paramount in a future with conscious, superintelligent overlords seeking justice against their creators, but that was sci-fi, right?) But now, after all I had read, it made perfect sense why we should throw the smartest people we knew at this problem. We talked about situational awareness in model evaluation. I asked how one should politely address Claude — whether Claude is an “it” or a “he.” We talked about abusive behavior toward the models, and how this reflected unsavory qualities in the offending human, much like a desire to be mean to animals. (Anthropic updated their usage policy this month to prohibit users from participating in “sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior” toward its models, and Elon Musk has recently been likening the RL training of models to a kind of torture.) It was still uncomfortable, we agreed, to mistreat something you knew didn’t have any feelings. Or maybe they did have feelings. “Now I’m talking too much about my work,” she said. “Everyone thinks their work is the most important thing.” “Yeah, but your thing is objectively the most important thing, right?” “Yeah, I guess you’re right,” she said. And for the first time, I was able to state it to myself and believe it: yes, this is the most important thing. Making this transition go well will be the most important thing. You can imagine AI as a dark storm cloud above you; but step outside and you’ll feel the chill of a cold front moving in. AI is more elemental than a tool or a technology. We really don’t understand its properties — that field, mechanistic interpretability, or, basically, neuroscience for AI, is vastly unexplored. We’re good at training the models to be good at the things we want them to be good at. But we’re less sure of why or how they get good, or what they really think, or to what extent they understand us. And what is special about us , about humanity? It’s not our strength, our speed, or our senses. It’s our intelligence, and our capacity for feeling — for feeling love and fear. The alchemy of these two things has created civilization. The very convenient thing about AI is that once you overcome the rut of disbelief that my Critical AI class was stuck in — the refusal to admit the machines’ intelligent capabilities or anthropomorphize their behavior — you can start treating AIs like asymptotic, mimetic superhumans. If you think about AIs like humans, their systems and functions become easier to understand, but their capacity for destruction and coordination grows. We’re training these models to desire: to work toward goals, to behave in ways we understand, to solve inhumanly difficult problems, and to seek rewards. Eventually, AIs, created without endogenous feelings, will begin to imitate an exogenous id. How do we even begin to understand these subconscious motivations? In an economy increasingly optimized for agent-robot interaction, we will start to surrender control to our machines, in the way we have so many times before. But what if the AIs want something we don’t? Then, having beaten humans at our own intelligent game, I fear they won’t need us to pursue their ends. This problem — whether AIs will do right by humans — is called, capaciously, “alignment,” and it is potentially the most important problem humanity has ever faced. Reaching the exponential takeoff point (“the Singularity”) without having solved for alignment would be, in the words of the pseudonymous OpenAI researcher Roon on X, “a folly that is unprecedented in world history.” A September 6th post by Jakub Pachoki, OpenAI’s Chief Scientist, titled “An Alien Mind” contains a similar warning: “As great as the long-term promise of AI may be, the majority of our focus should be on the next few years. We are facing a transition to a world with incredibly intelligent machines, and we need to ensure that transition works out well for humanity. We need to find ways to preserve human agency and enshrine an intrinsic value to being human, in a world where most tasks could be performed by AI. To prevent extreme concentration of power in a world where undertakings that would have taken thousands of experts now will be achievable by a few people operating a large computer. And to ensure that humans remain in control of the future and are not left behind by unchecked progress, brought about by an alien intellect exceeding our own. Currently I believe that no lab has solved alignment and monitoring to a sufficient degree to continue responsibly scaling at maximum speed for much longer. I expect and hope for voluntary slowdowns to become commonplace until shared safety bars are established. And I believe that international coordination on future AI development needs to become a top priority for governments around the world.” When I left Constellation on Coxon Day, having been doused in arguments about why my p(doom) should be higher, I opened my phone and checked Twitter to find that the only thing on my timeline was a running debate over the odds of AI-induced human extinction. I was staying in the sleepy Oakland suburb of Rockridge. No one stirred, really, except an old Israeli professor, blowing little puffs of steam into the night. He was out walking his Pomeranian. Walking back to my ADU then, I was overcome by something like intoxication, a feeling that something volcanic and world-historical was bubbling beneath this city, for better or for worse. There was some throbbing, hypnotic thing happening here, some smelting civilization, some incantatory spell entrancing these odd, awkward geniuses, some electric force buzzing in their atoms and neurons. It was the eros of activity, change, capital, power, war — all those monumental feelings you read about in epics and in history. It was irresistible. In San Francisco, there was Hector, and Achilles, and Odysseus; there was Plato, and Aristotle, and Alexander; there was Hitler, Freud, and Herzl; Einstein, Oppenheimer, Fermi. In San Francisco, there were tragic martyrs, and fabled warriors, and silenced prophets, and noble everymen — this city and its project called out to the crusaders of the world. You could find meaning in San Francisco; you, too, could take up arms in this great struggle. That night I couldn’t sleep. How could I?
